title: My day — and the little words that always sit in second place
goal: Talk about your daily routine, use *se* for actions that turn back on yourself, and master the strictest word-order rule in all of Slovenian: clitics (*naslonke*) always go in second place.
bekal: describing a routine from getting up to going to bed
putting *se*, *sem*, *mi*, *ga* in the right spot — second place, always

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Se ti mudi?
dialogs.intro: Maja and Budi are waiting for the bus. Budi realizes that the smallest words in Slovenian are the most stubborn ones.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: So what's your day usually like?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zbudim se ob šestih. Potem se stuširam.
lines.id: I wake up at six. Then I take a shower.
lines.literal: I-wake self at of-six. then self I-shower.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Tako zgodaj? Jaz se zbudim ob osmih.
lines.id: That early? I wake up at eight.
lines.literal: so early? I self I-wake at of-eight.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zajtrkujem doma, potem grem na univerzo.
lines.id: I have breakfast at home, then I head to the university.
lines.literal: I-breakfast at-home, then I-go to university.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: Are you in a rush in the mornings?

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Vedno. Nikoli si ne vzamem časa.
lines.id: Always. I never take my time.
lines.literal: always. never to-self not I-take of-time.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.text: Dobro poveš. In besedni red je pravilen.
lines.id: You say that well. And your word order is right.
lines.literal: well you-say. and word-of order is correct.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.text: Zakaj se ti mudi, ne ti se mudi?
lines.id: Why "se ti mudi" and not "ti se mudi"?
lines.literal: why self to-you hurries, not to-you self hurries?

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: Little words always jump to the front.

lines.speaker: Budi:
lines.id: Then I'll have to get used to it.

lines.speaker: Maja:
lines.id: You will. We all get used to it.

notes: **Se marks an action that turns back on the doer.** *Zbudim* means "I wake (someone else) up"; *zbudim **se*** means "I wake myself up", i.e. "I wake up". English handles some of this with "-self" or with a plain intransitive verb: get dressed, get used to it. The difference is that in Slovenian *se* is a separate word that moves around freely.

**And that's the catch: se never sits where you expect.** It belongs to the **clitics** (*naslonke*) — tiny unstressed words that must sit in **second place** in the sentence. Not after the subject, not before the verb: second place, counting from the start of the sentence.

**Nikoli si ne vzamem časa — negatives that don't cancel out.** *Nikoli* (never) and *ne* appear together, and that's compulsory. Slovenian insists the negation be repeated on the verb, just like Russian and Spanish. Dropping *ne* actually makes the sentence wrong.

**Zajtrkujem, kosim, večerjam — three meals, three verbs of their own.** Slovenian has separate verbs for having breakfast, lunch and dinner. The nouns are *zajtrk*, *kosilo*, *večerja*. You can say *jem zajtrk*, but Slovenians almost always use the verb.

**Se boš** (you will) is the future form, covered in full in unit 17. Notice that the main verb is dropped entirely because it's obvious from the previous sentence — a very Slovenian habit, and one that makes everyday conversation sound much shorter than the grammar would suggest.

grammars.title: Clitics — the second seat that nobody else may take
body: Slovenian has a group of tiny unstressed words: *se, si, sem, si, je, smo, ste, so, bi, me, te, ga, jo, jih, mi, ti, mu, ji*. They must all gather in **second place** in the sentence — after the first word or first phrase, whatever it happens to be.
after: The order inside the cluster is fixed too, and it never changes: **bi → sem/si/je → se → mi/ti/mu (indirect object) → me/te/ga/jo (direct object)**. So it's always *sem se*, never *se sem*; always *mu jo*, never *jo mu*.
If the sentence starts with a conjunction such as *da*, *ker*, *ki* or *če*, that conjunction counts as the first word: *Vem, **da se ti** mudi* (I know you're in a hurry).

grammars.title: Three verb endings: -am, -im, -em
body: Every Slovenian verb falls into one of three groups, and the only difference is a single vowel before the ending. The endings themselves — *-m, -š, -∅, -va, -ta, -mo, -te, -jo* — are always the same.
after: Notice that the dictionary form (*delati*, *govoriti*, *brati*) doesn't always tell you the group — *brati* ends in *-ati* but belongs to the *-em* group, and its "I" form even changes root to *berem*. So learn every verb in **two forms**: the dictionary form and the "I" form.
The *-am* group is the biggest and friendliest: almost all new verbs and loanwords go there. *Kliknem*, *guglam*, *parkiram* — they all follow the *delam* pattern.

sections.title: Moj dan — from getting up to going to bed

blocks.text: The sentences below run in order through a whole day. Say them all out loud once a day for a week, and you'll be able to describe your day without thinking.

Notice **grem spat** (I'm going to bed): *spat* is a special form that only appears after verbs of motion. *Grem jest* (I'm going to eat), *grem plavat* (I'm going swimming), *grem delat* (I'm going to work). It sounds very everyday, and using it just once makes your sentence sound natural right away.
And notice *kosim* — from *kosilo* (lunch), not from the word for mowing. Slovenian's three eating verbs: **zajtrkovati** (have breakfast), **kositi** (have lunch), **večerjati** (have dinner).
Frequency words move freely in the sentence, usually before the verb. But three of them drag *ne* into the sentence, and that's compulsory.

The last three rows are **stacked negatives**, and they feel strange exactly once. *Nikoli ne pijem piva* is literally "never not I-drink of-beer" — and notice that *pivo* becomes *piva* because the sentence is negative, just like the rule in unit 7. One sentence, two rules at once.

Standard English treats two negatives as cancelling each other out; Slovenian treats them as reinforcing each other. There's nothing to argue about — just accept that *ne* has to come along, and your sentence is instantly right.

blocks.title: Three sentences to use today
items: *Vsak dan se zbudim ob šestih.* — I wake up at six every day.
*Danes se mi ne mudi.* — I'm not in a hurry today.
*Nikoli ne zamujam.* — I'm never late. (Say it with a smile.)

exercises.prompt: Fill in the right form of the verb.
Put the words in the right order, with the clitics in the right place.

answers: zbudim — delaš — bere — spiva — kuhamo — gledajo

Koliko je ura? — Ura je pol treh. — Se dobiva ob petih? — Zamujam deset minut. — Nimam časa.
